sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
We first proposed the existence of this Source based solely on the evidence of the recent tectonic activity of the buried Ferrara Arc, highlighted by the control exerted on the evolution of the drainage network and by the geometry of syntectonic growth strata (Burrato et al., 2003). The 29 May 2012 Emilia earthquake, the second main shock of the Emilia sequence, activated this seismogenic source producing detectable uplift of the buried Mirandola anticline.
In the area located between the Pede-Apenninic Thrust front and the buried external fronts of the Northern Apennines an active compressional tectonic regime is documented by borehole breakout data with N-S oriented maximum horizontal stress, focal mechanism and GPS data. The focal mechanism of the 29 May 2012 earthquake was characterized by pure thrust faulting with conjugate planes oriented coherently with the strike of the mapped structures, and an horizontal P axis oriented N14.
The Pede-Apenninic Thrust Front is traditionally considered an active out-of-sequence thrust of the Northern Apennines belt, with a continuous trace along the Apennines foothills defined by geologic and geomorphic evidence of activity (e.g., Boccaletti and Martelli, 2004). However, recent papers proposed that the geomorphic feature of the pede-Apennines foothills is not the expression of a continuos shallow thrust fault (Picotti and Pazzaglia, 2008). According to this view, most of the regional deformation would be taken by a deep, blind thrust ramp responsible of the large scale geomorphology of the Northern Apennines foothills.
The ongoing activity of the more external Northern Apennines thrust fronts buried in the plain before the occurrence of the 2012 earthquake sequence was still a matter of debate, probable due to the unfavorable balance between tectonic activity (expressed as vertical deformation due to growing anticlines) and the rates of sedimentation. A direct consequence, is that only high resolution geophysical and geological subsurface data are able to detect the most recent growth of the buried structures.
Another process that masks the ongoing tectonic activity in the Po Plain is the differential compaction of unconsolidated sediments, that being proportional to the sediments' thickness mimicks the vertical tectonic movements induced by thrust activity (i.e. the relative sinclinal subsidence and anticlinal uplift).
The geometry of this Source and its kinematics were characterized by a combined study that as a first approach used the modeling of drainage anomalies and the backstripping of high-resolution stratigraphic data (Ciucci et al., 2002; Burrato et al., 2003; Scrocca et al., 2007).
In particular, the activity of this Source was responsible for attraction in the sincline and diversion around the anticline of the Secchia and Panaro rivers, whose paleo-courses show consistent evolution with migration towards areas of relative subsidence and away from the uplifting one. The use of high resolution stratigraphic data highlighted the geometry of growth strata in sintectonic strata, and allowed to calculate the relative uplift rates of the growing anticline during the late Quaternary, obtaining 0.16 mm/a of relative uplift rate for the last 125 ka (Scrocca et al., 2007).
The geometry and kinematics of this Source were further constrained after the occurrence of the 2012 earthquake sequence. On 20 and 29 May 2012 two earthquakes and their aftershocks sequence hit the central Po Plain about 40 km north of Bologna. During the seismic sequence pure compressional faulting was generated by the blind thrusts of the western Ferrara Arc, thereby activating a 50 km-long stretch of this buried outer front of the Northern Apennines. The focal mechanisms of the larger shocks agree with the compilation of present-day tectonic stress indicators showing in the area a ca. N-S oriented maximum horizontal stress, i.e. oriented perpendicular to the main structural trends. Most of the seismic sequence was confined between 1 and 12 km depth, above the local basal detachment of the outer thrust front of the Northern Apennines. Coseismic uplift of the ground surface produced by the two mainshocks registered by means of SAR interferometry is consistent with the pattern of the drainage anomalies identified by Burrato et al. (2003) (see also Burrato et al., 2012 and Bignami et al., 2012).
The rate of activity of the Mirandola thrust were studied using detailed subsurface geological data which shows growth geometry documenting uplift of the anticline during the last 0.65 Myr. After decompaction of the clastic units and modeling of the geometry of the sedimentary sequence were obtained slip rate values ranging between 0.80 and 1.15 mm/yr during the last 0.65 Myr (Maesano et al., 2013).
The coseismic anticline uplift was about 20 cm and the slip on the fault plane that resulted from the inversion of the SAR dataset was about 30 cm. A simple calculation using the coseismic slip and the slip rate calculated for the most recent time interval resulted in a return time estimates for earthquakes like the 2012 one.
We propose the following geometrical parameters for the source, which were constrained by modeling of the coseismic surface deformation registered by SAR and using seismological data:
- the strike is chosen according to the local strike of the buried Ferrara Arc constrained with modeling of the SAR data;
- the fault dips towards the South, according to subsurface seismic profiling; the rake is assumed to be pure thrusting, based on seismological evidence;
- the down-dip width is obtained by seismic profiles and is also constrained by modeling of the drainage anomalies;
- the minimum and maximum depth are constrained by subsurface geology and SAR modeling;
- the length is based on geological, geodetic and seismological data and constrained by modeling of the drainage anomalies.
This Source is associated with the 29 May 2012 earthquake; no other historical and/or instrumental earthquakes can be associated with it.
sections.SUMMARIES:
Castaldini et al. (1979)
In the framework of a reconstruction of neotectonic events, these workers examine the evolution of the drainage system of this reach of the Po Plain. The analysis considers the full length of the Holocene but special emphasis is given to the past three thousand years of progressive shift and sudden diversions of the main streams of the area. In particular, Castaldini et al. (1979) point out that the Secchia and Panaro rivers are first attracted towards each other and towards the axis of the so-called Bologna-Bomporto-Reggio Emilia syncline, then pushed sideways respectively towards the NW and E as they cross the alignment Carpi-Crevalcore. Castaldini et al. (1979) also describe important diversions that occurred after the VIII century B.C., particularly affecting the Po river turning North at Guastalla ("rotta di Guastalla"), the Secchia river turning East just North of Modena, and again the Secchia river turning northwest a few km South of Mirandola. Finally, Castaldini et al. (1979) describe surface faults in the area Mirandola-Concordia based on correlations of the stratigraphy of water wells, in the area of Canalazzo di Finale Emilia based on observations of open ground cracks aligned along a WNW trend, and near Correggio based on observations of fractures in walls and road pavements. This last fault is also seen in satellite imagery.
Veggiani (1985)
In the context of a reconstruction of paleo-channels of the Po river and of its main tributaries, this worker proposes a scheme for the evolution of the Secchia, Panaro, Crostolo and Reno rivers during the past 3,000 years. In particular, Veggiani (1985) proposes a dated sequence of progressive shifts of the Secchia and Panaro rivers up to their present position.
Cassano et al. (1986)
These investigators provide a comprehensive summary of subsurface and surface data along several transects crossing the Po Plain from the Southwest to the Northeast. Their interpretation of Section 9 shows a major anticline driven by a low-angle north-verging blind thrust culminating between Mirandola and Medolla.
Burrato et al. (2003)
These investigators analyzed in detail the fluvial system of the Po Plain and identify several areas where significant drainage anomalies (e.g., river diversions and shifts in channel patterns) with wave-length comparable to that of tectonic structures of crustal significance are suggestive of the presence of active blind thrust or reverse faults. As second step of their approach the authors compare the position of the drainage anomalies with the location of known buried anticlines, to corroborate the hypothesis of the tectonic nature of the anomalies. Following the observation that some of the anomalies are associated also with historical earthquakes, they propose that these blind thrusts may be potential sources of rather infrequent large earthquakes beneath the Po Plain.
Burrato et al show that the Secchio and Panaro rivers exhibit significant anomalies in their trend as they cross an anticline reported in the official geological map. They interpret the fluvial anomaly as having tectonic origin.

pictures.t: Paleochannels of Panaro and Secchia rivers
pictures.c: Recent evolution of the Panaro and Secchia rivers. South of the Mirandola Source both rivers are attracted towards the syncline; more to the North the Secchia R. is progressively shifted northwestward by the growing anticline (from Castaldini et al. [1979]).

Surface ruptures mapped by stratigraphic correlation of water wells and field surveys. They locate close to the hinge of the growing anticline and can therefore be interpreted as secondary extrados features (from Castaldini et al. [1979]).

pictures.t: Depth of fresh water-salt water interface
pictures.c: Fresh water-salt water interface in the Mirandola area, illustrating the spatial relationships between the buried anticline (to the NE) and the corresponding syncline (to the SW) (from Castaldini et al. [1979]).
Cross-section across the Mirandola anticline, showing extrados normal faulting dropping its northeastern limb and culmination of the marine deposits (from Panizza et al. [1987]).

pictures.t: Vertical movements in the Po Plain near Mirandola
pictures.c: Summary of inferred Holocene vertical movements in the area of the Panaro, Secchio and Po rivers, near Mirandola (from Panizza et al. [1987]).

pictures.t: Paleochannels of the Po River and main tributaries
pictures.c: Recent evolution of the Po River and its main tributaries. The thrust fault driving the Mirandola anticline is likely responsible for the attraction of the Panaro and Secchia rivers towards the syncline north of Modena, while the Po River appears to be shifted northward (from Veggiani [1985]).

pictures.t: Structural map of Po Plain and DISS v. 2.0
pictures.c: Simplified structural model of the Po Plain and cross-section showing the seismogenic sources included in the DISS v. 2.0. Individual seismogenic source ID 4 is the Mirandola thrust, at the time considered as a seismic gap. The source was identified using geomorphic and subsurface geological data (from Burrato et al. [2003]).
Geologic cross-section across Mirandola anticline (from Scrocca et al. [2007]).

pictures.t: Radarsat differential interferogram of the 2012 sequence
pictures.c: Radarsat-1 interferogram showing the coseismic ground uplift produced by the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes. The pattern of upift highlights the geometrical en-echelon relationships between the two seismogenic sources, and the vertical ground deformation of the Mirandola anticline. The simplified geological section shows the geometry at depth of the thrust fault source of the 29 May 2012 shock (from Bignami et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Cosmo-Sky Med interferograms of the 2012 sequence
pictures.c: COSMO-SkyMed interferogram and coseismic ground displacement maps of the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes. The red stars show epicenters of the M > 5 shocks occurred during the seismic sequence (from Salvi et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the Po Plain and its fluvial systems
pictures.c: Seismotectonic sketch showing the relationship between epicenters of the mainshocks of the 2012 seimic sequence, seismogenic sources of the DISS database and tectonic induced drainage anomalies (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Drainage anomalies in the epicentral area of the 2012 sequence
pictures.c: Declaration of a tectonic induced drainage anomaly: the buried Mirandola anticline induces the diversion of the Secchia and Panaro rivers (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Simplified geological section across 2012 epicentral area
pictures.c: Simplified geological section crossing the Mirandola anticline and the outer Ferrara Folds, and showing the proposed hypocenters of the two main shocks of the 2012 seismic sequence (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Drainage evolution of the central-southern Po Plain
pictures.c: Drainage evolution in the Po Plain south of the Po River. Tectonic growth of the buried Ferrara Folds induced the shift of the Secchia, Panaro, Reno and Po rivers. Drainage sudden diversions of the Po River in Guastalla (G) and Ficarolo (F) were controlled by major flood events after tectonic activity cumulated enough ground deformation (from Burrato et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Web based macroseismic intensities of the 29 May 2012 earthquake
pictures.c: Preliminary map of the macroseismic effects (MCS) of the 29 May 2012 earthquake (http://www.haisentitoilterremoto.it/). The data were collected using a web interface and were elaborated following the method proposed by Sbarra et al., 2010.

pictures.t: Compound macroseismic intensities of the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes
pictures.c: Map of the cumulated macroseismic intensities (EMS) of the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes (from Tertulliani et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Evolution of Mirandola Individual Source through time
pictures.c: The Mirandola source was initially identified and included in DISS (v. 2.0) using a geomorphic approach (source labelled A); its geometry was then refined using geophysical data (source B); the 29 May 2012 earthquake was generated by a segment of the Mirandola thrust (source C) partially coinciding with the fault first defined.

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the 2012 seismic sequence
pictures.c: Seismotectonic sketch of the 2012 seismic sequence with geological profile. Note that the coseismic deformation of the ground-surface caused by the 2012 sequence is consistent with the characteristic of the two 2012 seismogenic sources (from Vannoli et al. [2015]).
Geometric and kinematics parameters of the 20 and 29 May 2012 earthquakes as proposed by various investigators (from Vannoli et al. [2015]).
